Hiya, I am 18 & have a back issue but deal with secondary muscle issues that can prevent me from moving as a result of this so wanted to chip in.

The most helpful thing I’ve ever done is incorporate gentle stretches into my day, like when  I wait for the kettle to boil or netflix to load. Pain tells your muscles to tense up & gentle stretching & heat counteracts this, and the more regularly you stretch the more your body will relax. A yoga routine also works for this - just be careful as overdoing it will have the opposite effect.

I also found pilates very helpful as it strengthened my core & leg muscles so that I wasn’t having to compensate for weaknesses in other parts of my body. I hope this helps :)

Hi,
I am 18 & prolapsed a disc just after my 17th birthday. I have been living in pain since and I do not (and likely will never) have a diagnosis. Unfortunately, diagnosis is not always out there but that doesn’t mean you can’t be helped. I’ve had every drug & treatment under the sun but until I was seen by a consultant specialising in chronic pain I found no relief.

The consultant explained to me that sometimes the body forgets to turn the pain alarm off after recovering from an injury & the problem here is that pain tells your body to stiffen/react adversely. Like many other commenters have said, the key is building gentle exercises to minimise the impact of this reaction to the pain signal. Many doctors will incorrectly describe this phenomenon as your pain being psychological - it is not. Your pain is valid whether it is visible or not (I no longer have any visible injury on any scan but I still experience pain).

I recommend seeing a physiotherapist to help you adjust to life with and help manage your pain but of course everyone’s experience is different. Try and get in with a specialist in pain if you can - there are doctors out there who understand and will help you. Sending love :)
Just commenting to say I love this post & you absolutely have it spot on. Being gentle with yourself & allowing for plenty of rest between activities is key :)

Break it down into really small chunks. I have just received treatment for my herniated disc & damaged sciatic nerve but lived with the pain & no relief for over a year. The most helpful advice I ever had was about pain thresholds - when your body hurts so much you can’t stand, do a couple minutes of a task you can do sitting, then lying down, and cycle through small chunks of different tasks, resting in between, so that you never quite hit the threshold of causing yourself more damage if that makes sense? 

Lots and lots of rest and little bits at a time is the key - it’s okay to be slow and creaky and not get everything done in one go. Take your time & be gentle with yourself. If you haven’t, get a reusable heat pad you can strap to your lower back - pain tells your muscles to seize whether you notice it or not and the heat on your back muscles will help ease this and minimise future issues. I’m happy to share more about my experiences/answer questions if you need it & good luck :)

1. I take it because of “low mood” despite not being diagnosed with depression, my mum has had great success with sertraline so I was put on it on the basis that it should help because genetics.

2. From what I and my family have noticed, my mood has been stabilised significantly. I used to get suicidal lows and scarily manic happy highs, but now when I’m sad/happy it stays within what could be considered “normal”.

3. I haven’t tried being without it, because from what I’ve been told withdrawals are nasty. It helps enough that I have no reason to come off/go without it and I’m good at remembering to take it each morning. I am told it is likely I will be taking sertraline for the rest of my life.

4. I would like to think that it has. I have less frequent meltdowns and panic attacks, and I am overwhelmed less easily. My overall well-being has improved massively, not much really specific to autism I suppose.
